name: Propranolol Hydrochloride
sections: White crystalline powder (hydrochloride), soluble in water; melting point of base 96 °C; racemic mixture.

Developed by Sir James Black at ICI – the first successful beta-blocker, for which he shared the 1988 Nobel Prize in Medicine. First approval/introduction: Patented 1962; approved 1964 (ICI Pharmaceuticals).

Competitive antagonist at beta-1 and beta-2 adrenoceptors; reduces heart rate, myocardial contractility, renin release and sympathetic outflow; membrane-stabilising activity. Reduces somatic symptoms of anxiety and prevents migraine. Receptor / target profile: Non-selective competitive beta-1/beta-2 antagonist without intrinsic sympathomimetic activity; membrane-stabilising (sodium-channel) effect at high concentrations.
Extensive hepatic – CYP1A2, CYP2D6 (minor CYP2C19, CYP3A4); active 4-hydroxypropranolol
Summary: Well absorbed but extensive first-pass metabolism (bioavailability ~25%); Tmax 1–4 h (sustained-release longer). Lipophilic – crosses BBB. ~90% protein bound. Half-life 3–6 h (SR ~10 h).
Portal hypertension – prevention of variceal bleeding
Migraine prophylaxis: 40 mg two to three times daily, up to 80–160 mg/day; SR 80–160 mg once daily
Essential tremor: 40 mg two to three times daily; usual 80–160 mg/day
Anxiety: 40 mg once daily, up to three times daily
Hypertension: 80 mg twice daily initially, up to 160–320 mg/day
Dose to be individualised by the treating physician according to clinical response and tolerability.
Infantile haemangioma (specialist), arrhythmias, hypertension – weight-based dosing.
Use only if clearly needed; risk of fetal growth restriction, neonatal bradycardia and hypoglycaemia.
Bronchial asthma or history of bronchospasm
Sinus bradycardia, second/third-degree heart block, sick sinus syndrome
Do not stop abruptly – rebound angina/arrhythmia
Anaphylaxis may be more severe and resistant to adrenaline
Cimetidine, fluvoxamine (raise levels); rizatriptan (raise rizatriptan levels)
Take consistently with or without food (food increases bioavailability); avoid alcohol.
Heart rate, BP; glucose in diabetics; signs of heart failure.
Bradycardia, hypotension, bronchospasm, hypoglycaemia, seizures, coma. Atropine, glucagon, supportive care.
Cochrane review (Linde & Rossnagel, 2004) – propranolol effective for migraine prophylaxis.
BHAT (JAMA 1982) – propranolol reduced mortality after myocardial infarction.
Diabetics: may hide warning signs of low sugar
Store below 30°C in a dry place, protected from light and moisture. Keep out of the reach of children. Do not use after the expiry date.
